title: KV/prefix cache hit rate vs blended cost ($/1M output tokens) — analysis + anomaly notes
content:
Context / why this doc exists
- This is a working analysis to answer a recurring question in unit economics reviews: “When KV/prefix cache hit rate goes up, do we actually see blended $/1M output tokens go down?”
- Intended audience: serving-runtime + telemetry/analytics + Optimize. Finance will consume results indirectly via the Unit Economics dashboard once definitions are locked.
- Scope: Hosted + Dedicated traffic only (excluding Private deployments for now due to partial metering coverage and cost attribution differences). Output metric is blended $/1M output tokens as defined in the v1 methodology draft.


TL;DR (current findings, not a final conclusion)
1) We see a consistent negative relationship between cache hit rate and blended cost, but it’s weaker than expected and heavily confounded by batching efficiency + request mix (context length + output length).
2) In a “stable cohort” (same model/version, same region, same tier) cache hit rate improvements of +10pp correspond to ~3–8% reduction in blended $/1M output tokens, depending on batching regime.
3) The biggest anomalies (high hit rate but high cost) correlate with:
   - low batching utilization (queueing/arrival pattern changes)
   - long-context workloads (prefill dominates; cache helps, but not enough when prefill cost balloons)
   - streaming output token undercount periods (cost looks artificially high per output token)
4) Instrumentation gaps: hit rate definition is inconsistent across services (gateway vs runtime), and cache “eligibility” (requests that could have hit) is not measured consistently.


Definitions (please read; most confusion has been definitional)
- KV cache hit rate (runtime): fraction of tokens whose KV states were reused from cache rather than recomputed.
  - Current instrumentation mostly behaves like: hit_rate = reused_prefill_tokens / total_prefill_tokens
  - NOTE: this is not the same as “prompt prefix cache hit rate” at the application level.
- Prefix cache hit (logical): percent of requests where an initial prefix was served from cache (boolean per request).
  - We do not have a clean per-request boolean yet in analytics; we infer from token reuse counters.
- Blended $/1M output tokens:
  - Numerator: allocated GPU compute cost (and associated serving overhead as defined by FP&A rate card + allocation rules)
  - Denominator: metered output tokens (not input tokens)
  - Important: this means improvements that primarily reduce prefill compute (input-side) can still show up in $/output-token, but only if output token metering is stable and request mix isn’t shifting.


Data sources + time window
- Window: 2025-01-10 through 2025-02-15 (UTC day boundaries; we need to re-check Finance day boundary alignment later)
- Sources used:
  1) runtime metrics stream: kv_reused_tokens, kv_total_prefill_tokens, cache_evictions, cache_size_bytes
  2) request metering stream: output_tokens, input_tokens, streaming_flag, model_id/model_version, quantization_profile (partial)
  3) aggregation prototype views (Mei’s scratch SQL) for blended cost by {hour, model, region, tier}

Filters applied
- Excluded hours with known ingestion lag or “missing output tokens” alert (see Caleb’s notes in ENG-8421 thread)
- Excluded models with known model_id alias churn during the window (see model grouping aliases discussion; not resolved)
- Tier: self-serve + dedicated only
- Regions: us-east, us-west, eu-west (based on current region normalization draft; may still have “unknown”)


Graph 1 (time series): cache hit rate vs blended $/1M output tokens
Description of the plot
- X-axis: time (hourly)
- Left Y-axis: KV cache hit rate (0–1)
- Right Y-axis: blended $/1M output tokens (normalized index; 1.0 = period mean)
- Lines:
  - Blue: cache hit rate (smoothed with 6h moving average)
  - Red: blended cost index (smoothed with 6h moving average)

What we see
- In multiple weeks, we observe “mirror-ish” movement: cache hit rate up, cost down.
- However the cost line is noisier and exhibits spikes even when cache hit rate is stable.

Notes
- The cost spikes typically align with either (a) batching utilization drops, or (b) streaming metering changes (output token undercount makes cost per output token appear higher).


Graph 2 (scatter): hourly cache hit rate vs hourly blended cost (overall)
Description of the plot
- X-axis: hourly KV cache hit rate
- Y-axis: hourly blended $/1M output tokens
- Each dot = {hour, model_family} aggregated (weighted by output tokens)
- Color: region
- Shape: tier

What we see
- Clear negative slope overall, but wide variance.
- eu-west cluster sits higher cost at similar hit rates (expected due to rate card + utilization); us-east shows the widest spread.

Back-of-envelope stats (do not quote externally)
- Overall Pearson correlation (weighted by output tokens): ~ -0.32 to -0.45 depending on inclusion of “bad metering” hours
- When restricted to a stable cohort (below): improves to ~ -0.55


Graph 3 (cohort analysis): controlling for model/version + region + tier
Cohort definition
- model_id pinned to top-2 traffic models during the window (same version)
- quantization_profile pinned (where available; else infer from runtime config)
- region pinned (us-east)
- tier pinned (self-serve)

Description
- Scatter plot per cohort, plus simple linear regression line

What we see
- Relationship tightens materially.
- Regression slope suggests: +10 percentage points cache hit rate => ~3–8% improvement in blended $/1M output tokens.
  - The range depends on batching regime (see next graph).

Interpretation
- Cache helps, but is not the sole driver of blended cost; request mix and batching can dominate.


Graph 4 (interaction): cache hit rate vs cost, split by batching utilization bands
Batching utilization proxy
- We used a proxy from runtime metrics: avg_effective_batch_size / configured_max_batch (hourly average)
- Banding:
  - Low: < 0.35
  - Mid: 0.35–0.65
  - High: > 0.65

Description
- Same scatter as Graph 3, but faceted into three panels by batching band

What we see
- In High batching hours, cache hit rate improvements translate more directly into cost improvements.
- In Low batching hours, cache hit rate appears “less effective” (cost stays high even at decent hit rates).

Hypothesis
- When batching is poor, GPU time per token is dominated by scheduling/fragmentation/underutilization overhead, so cache savings are diluted.


Key anomalies and working hypotheses
Anomaly A: High cache hit rate but higher blended cost (especially in eu-west)
- Observed pattern: eu-west shows higher cost at similar hit rates even after cohorting.
- Hypotheses:
  1) Rate card differences (expected): eu-west GPU hour cost higher; this should be “real.”
  2) Region utilization / idle allocation: if idle capacity allocation is higher in eu-west during low traffic, blended cost inflates.
  3) Region normalization gaps: some eu-west traffic may be mis-bucketed, blending with a higher cost pool.

Anomaly B: Cache hit rate rises, but cost does not improve (flat or worsens)
- Observed around specific days when streaming adoption increased.
- Hypotheses:
  1) Streaming output token undercount (known issue): denominator shrinks, $/output-token rises. This can fully invert the apparent relationship.
  2) Output-length shift: more short answers (fewer output tokens) can worsen blended $/output-token even if compute is down, depending on how overhead is allocated.

Anomaly C: Hit rate drops sharply, but cost barely moves
- Hypotheses:
  1) Cache hit rate metric is mostly prefill reuse; if workload is decode-heavy (large outputs), prefill savings don’t move total cost much.
  2) Measurement mismatch: we’re comparing runtime cache hit rate to blended cost computed per output token; when output dominates, prefill-only improvements are muted.

Anomaly D: Very high hit rates (>0.85) on hours where we don’t expect it
- Hypotheses:
  1) Metric bug: reused_prefill_tokens counter may include tokens from same-request reuse (not true cross-request caching) in some code paths.
  2) Eligibility problem: denominator excludes “non-cacheable” requests inconsistently, inflating hit rate.


What I think is true vs what is still uncertain
Likely true (based on current evidence)
- Cache hit rate is directionally helpful and correlates negatively with blended cost.
- Batching utilization and request mix (context length distribution) can dominate and must be included in any “explain the week” narrative.

Uncertain / needs follow-up
- The “true magnitude” of cache savings on $/1M output tokens is not well estimated without:
  - clean token metering parity (especially streaming)
  - a cache eligibility metric
  - better prefill/decode ratio instrumentation in analytics


Recommendations (instrumentation + dashboard)
1) Add cache eligibility + per-request prefix_hit boolean
- Proposed metrics:
  - prefix_cache_eligible_requests
  - prefix_cache_hit_requests
  - prefix_cache_hit_rate_requests = hit_requests / eligible_requests
- Rationale: token-level hit rate is hard to interpret and can be inflated by denominator quirks.

2) Standardize hit rate definition across runtime/gateway
- Write down a single canonical definition and emit both the numerator and denominator explicitly.
- Don’t just emit “hit_rate” as a precomputed gauge; emit counters and compute in aggregation.

3) Add prefill/decode ratio to the unit economics view
- This will explain why cache impact disappears on long-context workloads.
- Proposed: prefill_tokens, decode_tokens, ratio = prefill_tokens/(prefill_tokens+decode_tokens)

4) Dashboard “explainers”
- On the Unit Economics dashboard, add an “Attribution signals” panel with:
  - cache hit rate (and definition)
  - batching utilization proxy
  - avg input length, avg output length
  - streaming share
  - prefill/decode ratio
- Add a footnote: “Cache hit rate is primarily a prefill reuse metric; interpret alongside prefill/decode ratio.”


Action items / owners (draft)
- [Nadia] Align on a canonical cache hit rate definition (runtime + telemetry). Target: end of next week.
- [Caleb] Provide a list of “bad metering” hours (streaming undercount + ingestion gaps) to exclude from analysis and later to power confidence indicators.
- [Mei] Add a prototype field to the aggregation views for batching utilization band and prefill/decode ratio (even if partial).
- [Sean] Validate whether eu-west cost deltas are driven by idle allocation vs rate card vs utilization; propose how to present this in exec readouts.


Appendix A: quick table of notable days (for cross-referencing with incidents)
Date (UTC) | Symptom | Notes
- 2025-01-18 | cost spike with stable hit rate | batching utilization dipped; check queueing
- 2025-01-27 | hit rate up, cost up | suspected streaming output token undercount window
- 2025-02-03 | eu-west outlier cluster | likely rate card + lower utilization; needs confirmation
- 2025-02-10 | hit rate cliff | cache eviction surge (config?) but blended cost flat (decode-heavy period)


Appendix B: caveats
- This is not causal inference. We are correlating aggregated signals and are sensitive to confounds (batching, mix shifts, metering bugs).
- Blended cost allocation method may change (idle capacity treatment / overhead). If allocation changes, slopes and correlation will change even if runtime performance is constant.
- For exec/Finance reporting, we should not over-index on cache hit rate alone; it’s one lever among several.
